newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Citibank sees bank gold selling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Citibank sees bank gold selling.

text.p: Central banks have been recent sellers of gold and may be preparing to unload more, the global head of precious metals for Citibank said on Thursday.
Central banks sales of gold have been "on the horizon for some time" leading up to changes in the European monetary system, Sydney-based Chris Fehon told Reuters in an interview.

Despite widespread belief that gold producers were behind recent waves of selling that hammered gold to three-year lows of less than US$366.00 an ounce earlier this week, the central banks were more likely sellers, Fehon said.
The price has since rebounded to around US$370.00 an ounce.
"It (selling) seems to be coming out of Europe more than anywhere," Fehon said.

"The intelligence we've had is that its generally not coming from producers...," he said. "We can only presume its either new positioning going short through the speculators or, more likely some central bank disposals," Fehon said.
The world's central banks hold an estimated 35,000 tonnes of gold -- more than is produced worlwide in 10 years -- but have been under pressure to exchange metal for other investments.
"It's certainly possible sales are going to increase going forward," Fehon said.
Fehon said he would not be surpised if central banks were selling gold to meet European monetary convergence criteria, but said he said he had no evidence of that occurring yet.
"Gold appears to be less well regarded internationally as a reserve asset, particularly in this low-inflation environment," Fehon said.
He said he does not expect much fund activity in the gold market in the next several months after a busy second half.
"They came into this market hoping they'd see a significant sell off, which they have," he said.
Gold also faces a rough ride in developing economies as more sophisticated investment tools are introduced, he said.
"Particularly as the economies develop and their access to markets improve... gold could become less important than it is now," he added.
But presently, Asia maintains an appetite for gold, he said.
"For now we're seeing quite good investment demand for hoarding in Asia," Fehon said.
"It's going to be a very slow process for that to change."
Turning to price, Fehon said central bank inventories and other hoardings have virtually wiped any floor price for gold.
"Structually, gold does not have floor because you could have no production and still have sufficient supplies coming from the above-ground stockpiles," Fehon said.
Recent increases in lease rate interest charges from around one percent to near three percent are having a positive impact on the gold market, Fehon said.

Lease rates are interest charged by banks to lend gold to the market. As lease rates go up, making it more expensive to borrow gold, some producers may be less inclined to forward sell future mine production.
"The benefit of forward selling is less than if rates were still at one percent," Fehon said.
"This has provided quite a break on producer selling," he said. "It's eating heavily into their contango."
As a result, producers have been less agressive in placing forward positions in 1996 than in previous years, Fehon said.
In Australia, any producers inclined to unwind probably have already done so, Fehon said.

"People that didn't unwind, I don't think they will ever unwind ... because the short-term fluctuations in the value of the program don't really reflect their commitment to the program," Fehon said. Fehon also said seasonal sales of gold were looking flat this year, due to uncertainty among consumers.
Citibank's worldwide precious metals operations are based in Sydney.
